clue.text: Who wrote fantastic Gothic oeuvre, never wanting energy?

definitions.text: Who wrote fantastic Gothic oeuvre, never wanting energy?

indicators.note: A fantasy has no obligation to the shape of the real thing, and letters called fantastic keep none of their given order.
To want a thing here is to lack it, and 'never' pushes the lack all the way: not one of those letters may survive.

parts.note: E is the physicist's symbol for energy, and the French word holds two of them — both are what leave
the ten letters left once the E's have gone — G, O, T, H, I, C, O, U, V, R — rearranged into the novelist

explanation.walkthrough: Notre-Dame de Paris is the Gothic novel behind the surface, and its author was famously prolific. Italics in a clue usually flag a foreign word.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: Hugo wrote Notre-Dame de Paris, a Gothic novel of huge scope, and was famously tireless at his desk.

clue.text: Very big and very secure, but lacking function

indicators.note: Something lacking is short of a part it ought to have, so the letter named beside it is simply never written down.

parts.note: f(x) — f is the mathematician's letter for a function, and it is the letter that goes
v is the everyday abbreviation for very, as in v. good
secure is fast, as in held fast; take the f off the front and these three letters are what remain

explanation.walkthrough: Two single letters standing for whole words in four squares. V for very and F for function are both worth banking — short clues are mostly built out of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Very big → VAST: the word is kept for expanses — a vast plain, a vast fortune — so it means big in extent rather than merely large.

clue.text: Sour-tempered type, conservative, upset drinking establishment

parts.note: C is the ballot-paper abbreviation for the Conservative party

indicators.note: A thing upset has been tipped over, and a word tipped over in a down clue is read from the bottom up.

parts.note: a bar is where the drinking is done, and it is what gets tipped over

explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'conservative' looks like punctuation in a list of insults and is really the join between two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Sour-tempered type → CRAB: a crab is a peevish grumbler, the sense that survives in 'crabby' and in crosswords more than in speech.

clue.text: Actor veered off and got upset about nothing

indicators.note: Milk that has gone off has turned into something other than itself, and so have these letters.

parts.note: the eleven letters of ACTOR VEERED, taken in a new order

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sells you a temperamental actor, and the definition hides at the far end of the sentence still sounding like more of the anecdote.
explanation.definitionFit: got upset about nothing → OVER-REACTED: reacting out of all proportion to the cause, so the size of the fuss is the fault rather than the anger.

clue.text: Take courage and judicially try X

parts.note: a court hears a case, which is what trying it judicially means
X is ten in Roman numerals, which is why the setter has set it in italics

explanation.walkthrough: An italicised single letter is nearly always a numeral or a symbol rather than the letter itself, and X is the one you meet most.
explanation.definitionFit: Take courage → HEARTEN: the verb's intransitive side, to grow bolder — the same idea as 'take heart', with the noun made into a verb.

clue.text: Exhortation to make a nag depart?

definitions.meaning: the general sense: a cry urging somebody to get moving, used now far away from any stable
the original job of that cry — what a driver calls to a horse to set it going

explanation.walkthrough: A nag is a horse and also a person who goes on at you, and the clue is happy for you to hear the second one first.
explanation.definitionFit: Both halves land on one cry: it is an exhortation in the plain sense of urging somebody on, and specifically the command that starts a horse.

clue.text: Chooses, therefore, to go back to grasp point

indicators.note: Going back along an across answer means travelling right to left, so the word is written the other way round.
To grasp a thing is to close your hand round it, so what follows sits inside rather than after.

parts.note: therefore is so, and it is the word that gets turned round
pt is the standard abbreviation for point, on a map and on a scoreboard alike

explanation.walkthrough: Four squares and two abbreviations. Collecting the small ones — so, pt, v, n — is most of what makes short clues quick.
explanation.definitionFit: Chooses → OPTS: to opt for something is to choose it, the verb setters reach for whenever a decision has to fit four letters.

clue.text: Red tea and ripe bananas in second home

indicators.note: To go bananas is to lose your reason, and letters that have lost theirs will not stay in sensible order.

parts.note: six letters of the mixture, hiding in a plausible drink
four more, and the word that makes the fruit of the surface work

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a fruit bowl and the definition is two flat words at the end. The French phrase means literally 'foot on the ground'.
explanation.definitionFit: second home → PIED-A-TERRE: a small flat kept in town for occasional nights, so it is a base rather than a house you live in.

clue.text: Bird sweeps up structure containing insects

indicators.note: The sense of 'what's up' — something is amiss — and letters that are amiss have left their proper order.

parts.note: the ten letters of BIRD SWEEPS, resettled

explanation.walkthrough: Spiders are not insects, which is what makes the definition exact rather than sloppy: the maker is one thing and the catch is another.
explanation.definitionFit: structure containing insects → SPIDER'S WEB: the web is a trap built to catch and hold them, so the definition names it by what it collects.

clue.text: Agree to unnerve crew

parts.note: to shake somebody is to unnerve them, to leave them rattled
hands are a ship's crew — all hands on deck

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hands' for a crew is worth keeping: it is one of the sea words setters never let go of, and here it lands on a gesture instead of a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: Agree → SHAKE HANDS: the gesture that seals a bargain, so the phrase stands for reaching agreement rather than for the movement itself.

clue.text: Finally obtained some delightful salami — here?

indicators.note: What comes finally is what comes at the end, and here it is the end of each word rather than the end of the sentence.

parts.note: the last letter of each word in turn: obtaineD, somE, delightfuL, salamI

explanation.walkthrough: One indicator can govern a whole run of words, not just the one beside it. The dash before the definition is the setter pointing at the shop.
explanation.definitionFit: here → DELI: the counter you would be standing at while buying the salami, so the clue names the shop by pointing at itself.

clue.text: Prepay and settle rent, prithee

indicators.note: This is the past participle of rend, meaning torn — so what stands before it has been ripped out of shape.

parts.note: six letters of the mixture
six more, and a second word that sounds like paying a bill

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a landlord's demand and the answer is a child's wheedle, which is about as far apart as two readings of five words get.
explanation.definitionFit: prithee → PRETTY PLEASE: the archaic 'pray thee' is a coaxing request, and the modern phrase is the same coaxing with an intensifier stuck on.

clue.text: Players in starring roles the reader ennobled, we hear

definitions.note: A club is one thing and 'Players' is many, but British football speaks of a team in the plural — the definition names the eleven rather than the badge.

indicators.note: What is heard need not be what is written, so both halves are to be taken by sound.

parts.note: the starring roles in a production are the LEADS, and said aloud that spells a Yorkshire city
the reader is YOU, and to ennoble is to knight — YOU KNIGHTED said aloud is a football suffix

explanation.walkthrough: Setters address the solver as 'the reader' or 'you' constantly, and spotting that is often the whole step.
explanation.definitionFit: Players → LEEDS UNITED: definition by example, one club standing in for a set of footballers, and British usage lets the club name take a plural.

clue.text: Flip over and unwisely flutter runt that's not strong

indicators.note: Doing a thing unwisely is doing it without judgement, and letters handled without judgement come back in no sensible arrangement.

parts.note: f is forte in a score, the mark for strong, so denying strength takes that letter away
with the f gone, the ten letters left are shuffled

explanation.walkthrough: 'Strong' at the end of a clue is very often a single letter leaving rather than an adjective doing any describing.
explanation.definitionFit: Flip over → TURN TURTLE: sailors' idiom for a boat capsizing so completely that the hull ends up on top, like a turtle on its back.

clue.text: In announcement, manifest seams of ore as can be aerially transported

definitions.note: The setter defines an amount by what will fit in one aircraft rather than by a plural noun, which is how a measure comes to stand for countable loads.

indicators.note: An announcement is made to the ear rather than to the page, so the words are to be taken by sound.

parts.note: manifest means plain, obvious; PLAIN said aloud is spelt as an aircraft
a lode is a vein of ore in rock, so seams of ore are LODES, spelt as cargo

explanation.walkthrough: 'Manifest' is doing double duty on the surface, since a manifest is also the list of what an aircraft is carrying. 'Mother lode' is where the ore word survives.
explanation.definitionFit: as can be aerially transported → PLANELOADS: the noun measures cargo by the aircraft carrying it, the way 'busloads' measures people.

clue.text: Completely forget number Lauren arranged

indicators.note: To arrange is to put things in an order somebody chose, and the order chosen is not the one they came in.

parts.note: n is the standard abbreviation for a number, as in n items
the name hands over all six of its letters

explanation.walkthrough: A first name in a clue is usually raw material rather than a person. Notice how much work 'completely' is doing in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Completely forget → UNLEARN: not mere forgetting but deliberately undoing a lesson, the un- prefix cancelling something that was once known.

clue.text: Detectives who'll prepare potatoes?

definitions.meaning: Victorian slang for the police, coined from the name of the man who founded them
the literal reading: the little blades that take the skin off before boiling

explanation.walkthrough: Sir Robert Peel set up the Metropolitan Police in 1829 and his men were peelers and bobbies from the start. The question mark admits the kitchen sense is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Peelers was the Victorian nickname for Peel's police, covering the force and its detectives; the other sense is literal, the tools that skin potatoes.

clue.text: Section of canon's to play on a loop

indicators.note: A section is a piece cut out of something longer, so the letters are already sitting in the words that follow.

parts.note: the run starts partway into the first word and ends one letter into the last, crossing the apostrophe as if it weren't there

explanation.walkthrough: Hidden answers love a possessive: the apostrophe in 'canon's' is invisible to the letters, so the run carries straight across it.
explanation.definitionFit: on a loop → NON-STOP: something played on a loop restarts the instant it ends, so it runs with no break in it at all.

clue.text: Mischievous, like element of ice-hockey game?

parts.note: the hard rubber disc the whole game is played with
-ish is the ending that turns a noun into 'somewhat like it'

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay points at the rink and the meaning points at Shakespeare — Puck is the sprite of A Midsummer Night's Dream, and the two are unrelated.
explanation.definitionFit: Mischievous → PUCKISH: Puck is that tricksy sprite, so the adjective means impish in his particular teasing way rather than merely naughty.

clue.text: Old boy to wait at table and make remarks?

parts.note: OB is the school register's shorthand for an old boy
to serve is what waiting at table amounts to

explanation.walkthrough: The definition looks like the tail of the same restaurant scene, which is why it is easy to read past it and keep hunting.
explanation.definitionFit: make remarks → OBSERVE: the sense in 'he observed that it was late' — to say something aloud, the far end of the word from watching.

clue.text: Partially uncoils kinks in outerwear

indicators.note: Only part of what follows is wanted, so the letters are a stretch taken out of the middle of it.

parts.note: the run straddles the gap between the two words, unbroken across the space

explanation.walkthrough: A hidden answer that crosses a word boundary is the hardest kind to see, because the eye reads whole words before it reads letters.
explanation.definitionFit: outerwear → OILSKIN: a coat of oil-treated cloth pulled on over everything else at sea, so it is named for its waterproofing.

clue.text: Subject of a swan song?

parts.note: the surface offers a farewell performance, an artist's last work; the setter means a tale that finishes with a swan in it
the creature the story follows, jeered at in the farmyard until it grows into what it was all along

explanation.walkthrough: There are no letters to assemble here, only a phrase read the other way round. Knowing the Andersen story is the whole solve.
explanation.definitionFit: Andersen's tale ends with the derided bird finding it is a swan, so the story really is a song about one, and this is its hero.

clue.text: General idea is tucking into G&T

indicators.note: To tuck something in is to push it inside and close the gap over it, which is where the shorter word ends up.

parts.note: a G&T is a gin and tonic, and its two initials are what sit outside
the little verb goes in whole, letters and all

explanation.walkthrough: A drink written as initials is two capitals with a gap in the middle, which is exactly the shape a container clue wants.
explanation.definitionFit: General idea → GIST: the gist is the pith of what was said, the essential drift you would give if asked to summarise it briefly.

clue.text: Eager to wail

definitions.meaning: the everyday adjective for someone enthusiastic about an idea or itching to start
a quite separate verb, borrowed from Irish, for the lament raised over a body

explanation.walkthrough: Four letters and two words that share nothing but their spelling. The Irish verb comes from 'caoinim', and it is the one crosswords lean on.
explanation.definitionFit: Eager is the plain adjective; the other sense is a verb from Irish, to raise the drawn-out wailing lament at a wake.

clue.text: Title socialists avidly revoked, primarily!

indicators.note: What is primary comes first, so what is taken from each word is the letter standing at its head.

parts.note: the initials of the four words in order: Title Socialists Avidly Revoked

explanation.walkthrough: An initial-letter clue that also reads as plain history is the prize of the genre, and the history here is right: the last holder was deposed in 1917.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: an imperial rank that revolutionaries abolished, so the words describing it are also the words spelling it.

clue.text: We come to work? Yes and no

definitions.text: We come to work? Yes and no

parts.note: as an answer to a question it sounds shifty; said by strikers it is plain fact — they are at the gate at the usual hour
the qualification is the joke: they turn up at the place of work without doing any of it

explanation.walkthrough: No wordplay to find — 'we' is the strikers speaking. A clue in the first person nearly always means the answer is the speaker or the spot they stand on.
explanation.definitionFit: Strikers gather outside the workplace they are refusing to enter, so the honest answer to 'do we come to work' is genuinely both at once.

clue.text: Principally, Everyman, more than once, pronouncedly moderate

indicators.note: The principal of anything is the one at the head of it, so what is taken is the letter at the head of the word.
On the surface it means markedly, but its root is 'pronounce' — the letters are to be said rather than read.

parts.note: the letter at the head of Everyman is E, and more than one E is E's — say that aloud and you have spelt the answer

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman puts his own name into a clue most weeks, and it is worth only its first letter here. The commas make a pile of instructions look like a description.
explanation.definitionFit: moderate → EASE: the verb sense, since to ease a restriction is to moderate it, rather than the noun meaning comfort or leisure.

clue.text: Made little effort: piano sharp (that's one element)

parts.note: p is piano in a score, the musician's mark for soft
a honed blade is a sharp one
I is one in Roman numerals
tin is element 50, and the bracket is what points at the periodic table

explanation.walkthrough: 'Piano' and 'sharp' both look musical and only one of them is. P for soft is among the most-used single letters in cryptics, so it is worth banking early.
explanation.definitionFit: Made little effort → PHONED IT IN: the performer's idiom for delivering a part down a wire instead of turning up, so the job is done without engagement.
